title: Colorado AI Act and hiring: what employers must do from 2027
description: How Colorado's AI law affects hiring in 2027: SB 26-189 replaced the 2024 act, which hiring tools are covered, required notices, explanations, human review and records, and the draft rules.
short: Colorado's SB 26-189, effective January 1, 2027, replaces the 2024 Colorado AI Act. Employers using AI that materially influences hiring decisions must give notice, explain rejections within 30 days, allow data correction and human review, and keep records for three years.
body:
On January 1, 2027, Colorado's rules for automated hiring decisions take effect. They are not the rules most HR teams read about in 2024. In May 2026 the legislature passed SB 26-189, and Governor Polis signed it on May 14, 2026, replacing the original Colorado AI Act before it ever applied. According to Ogletree's summary of the new law, the duty of care, risk management program and impact assessment requirements are gone. In their place are notice, explanation, correction and human review duties that land directly on employers who use AI in hiring.

This explainer covers what changed, which hiring tools are in scope, what employers will have to do, and what the attorney general's draft rules add. It is a summary, not legal advice.

What the law covers

The law applies to covered automated decision making technology that materially influences a consequential decision. Employment is one of the decision areas, alongside education, housing, lending, insurance, health care and essential government services. Ogletree notes that the protected group includes employees, job applicants who live in Colorado and people evaluated for opportunities in the state, so an employer headquartered elsewhere can still be covered when it hires for Colorado roles.

"Materially influences" is the key test. A tool is in scope when its output is a non trivial factor that affects the outcome, for example by scoring, ranking or recommending candidates. Tools that only summarize, organize or display information for a person to review are treated differently, which matters for resume parsers and interview notetakers that do not score anyone. Our explainer on ATS and AI resume screening walks through which screening features rank and which only sort.

What employers will have to do

Based on the statute as summarized by Ogletree, an employer that uses a covered tool in hiring will need to:

  • Give candidates a notice before the tool is used.
  • Explain an adverse outcome, such as a rejection, within 30 days, including the role the technology played.
  • Let candidates correct inaccurate personal data used by the tool and, where commercially reasonable, request meaningful human review of the decision.
  • Keep records for at least three years.

Meaningful human review has a specific meaning. The reviewer must have authority to change the outcome, must consider the relevant evidence, must be trained, must not simply defer to the system's output and must understand the tool's intended use and limits. A recruiter who clicks approve on every AI shortlist does not meet that bar.

Vendors, staffing firms and contracts

Developers of covered tools must give deployers the documentation they need to meet these duties. Ogletree also reports that contract clauses that try to make one party indemnify the other for its own discrimination violations are void. In practice, employers should expect new vendor paperwork and should review indemnity terms in AI hiring contracts before renewal.

Using a staffing agency does not move the problem elsewhere. A National Law Review article from November 3, 2026 describes a draft rule example in which a staffing firm supplies an AI generated shortlist and the hiring employer is still responsible as the deployer.

The attorney general's draft rules

The Colorado attorney general is writing implementing rules. As Orrick explained on JD Supra, proposed rules were released in August 2026, an interim redline followed on October 6, and a rulemaking hearing was held on October 26. The drafts add detail that matters for recruiting teams:

  • A presumption that a tool materially influenced a decision when a person reviewed its score, ranking or recommendation and the final decision matched it. An employer can rebut the presumption by showing the output was a de minimis factor.
  • More specific adverse outcome explanations, including what the technology did.
  • Human reviewers can be internal staff or outside reviewers, as long as they can actually override the result.
  • Clear, plain language notices and an inventory of covered tools.

The rules were still in draft as of November 11, 2026, so details may change before January.

Enforcement

Only the attorney general can enforce the law; there is no private right of action. Ogletree reports a 60 day cure period for most violations, except knowing or repeated ones, and the National Law Review article describes the cure period as running until January 1, 2030. Existing discrimination claims under state and federal law remain available to candidates, so a biased tool is still a legal risk even when the new procedural duties are met.

A checklist for hiring teams

  1. List every tool that scores, ranks, filters or recommends candidates for Colorado roles.
  2. Ask each vendor for its developer documentation and how the tool reaches its output.
  3. Draft the pre use notice and an adverse outcome template that names the tool's role.
  4. Name and train human reviewers who can override results.
  5. Set up data correction requests and three year record retention.
  6. Review indemnity and allocation clauses in vendor and staffing contracts.

For how Colorado fits alongside New York City's audit rules and other regulation, read the guide chapter on bias, regulation and candidate rights, and for the screening tools most likely to be covered, see AI phone screening and AI interviewers.

faq.q: When does the Colorado AI Act apply to hiring?
faq.a: The replacement law, SB 26-189, takes effect on January 1, 2027. The original 2024 Colorado AI Act was repealed and replaced before it took effect.

faq.q: Does the Colorado AI law still require impact assessments?
faq.a: No. SB 26-189 removed the duty of care, risk management program and impact assessment requirements. It focuses on notice, adverse outcome explanations, data correction, human review and records.

faq.q: Which hiring tools are covered in Colorado?
faq.a: Tools that materially influence a hiring decision, for example by scoring, ranking or recommending candidates. Tools that only summarize or organize information for a person to review are treated differently.

faq.q: Can candidates sue under the Colorado AI law?
faq.a: No. The attorney general enforces it and there is no private right of action, but candidates can still bring discrimination claims under existing law.

faq.q: Is an employer responsible if a staffing agency uses the AI?
faq.a: Under the attorney general's draft rules, yes in the example described: when a staffing firm supplies an AI generated shortlist, the employer that relies on it is still responsible as the deployer.

title: EU AI Act and recruitment: what hiring teams must do, and when
description: How the EU AI Act applies to recruitment after the 2026 Digital Omnibus: which hiring tools are high risk, the new 2 December 2027 date, deployer duties, GDPR Article 22 and what to do now.
short: The EU AI Act classes AI used to advertise jobs, filter applications or evaluate candidates as high risk. The 2026 Digital Omnibus moved those obligations to 2 December 2027, but the bans and AI literacy rules already apply, and GDPR Article 22 still governs automated hiring decisions today.
body:
Three dates matter for anyone using AI to hire in the European Union: 2 February 2025, when the AI Act's bans took effect; 2 December 2026, when a second round of transparency and prohibition changes lands; and 2 December 2027, the new date for the high risk rules that cover most recruitment software. The middle and last dates are recent. They come from Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, which was adopted on 8 July 2026, published in the Official Journal on 24 July and in force from 27 July, as summarised in an EY legal alert.

This explainer covers what the AI Act means for recruiters and talent teams after that amendment. It is not legal advice; check your own setup with counsel.

Which recruiting tools count as high risk

Annex III of the AI Act lists employment as a high risk area. The recruitment entry covers AI systems intended to be used for recruiting or selecting people, in particular to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates. A second entry covers decisions about promotion, termination, task allocation and monitoring or evaluating workers, as Ogletree lays out.

In practice that reaches resume screeners and ranking engines, AI interview scoring, chat or phone screeners that decide who moves forward, sourcing tools that rank candidates for a role, and ad platforms that choose who sees a job. A scheduling assistant that only books a slot, or a writing aid for job descriptions, is usually outside the list because it does not evaluate people. Our explainer on ATS and AI resume screening shows where screening logic tends to sit inside these tools.

What the Digital Omnibus changed

The original Act applied the Annex III high risk rules from 2 August 2026. The Omnibus postponed them to 2 December 2027, and moved high risk safety components in regulated products, under Annex I, to 2 August 2028. Per EY, it also narrowed the definition of a safety component, softened the AI literacy duty in Article 4 from ensuring a level of literacy to taking measures that promote it, added a legal basis for limited processing of special category data to detect and correct bias, and added two new prohibited practices covering AI that generates non consensual intimate images or child sexual abuse material.

Those new bans, and the Article 50(2) duty to mark AI generated content for systems already on the market before 2 August 2026, apply from 2 December 2026, according to CASRAI's summary of the regulation. For most hiring teams the marking rule falls on vendors of generative tools, not on employers, but it will show up in contract updates this winter.

What already applies today

The delay does not make recruitment AI unregulated in the meantime. The Article 5 bans have applied since 2 February 2025, and one of them targets the workplace directly: emotion recognition in workplaces is prohibited except for medical or safety reasons. A video interview tool that infers enthusiasm or stress from a candidate's face is the obvious risk. Biometric categorisation that infers sensitive traits such as race or political views is also banned.

GDPR also applies in full. Article 22 gives people the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing that significantly affects them, with exceptions for explicit consent, contract necessity and authorisation by law. On 11 November 2026 the European Data Protection Board said its 2027 coordinated enforcement action will review Article 22 compliance and the right of access for automated decision making in employment, including candidate screening tools, as reported by IAPP. Data protection authorities will be asking employers about screening tools well before the AI Act's high risk date.

Provider or deployer: who does what

The Act splits duties between the provider, who builds the system and places it on the market, and the deployer, who uses it. Most employers are deployers. Vendors carry the heavier load: risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, accuracy and robustness testing, a conformity assessment, CE marking and registration in the EU database.

From 2 December 2027, an employer deploying a high risk hiring tool must, under Article 26:

  • use it according to the provider's instructions for use
  • assign human oversight to people with the competence, training and authority to override it
  • make sure input data it controls is relevant and sufficiently representative
  • monitor the system and report serious incidents or risks to the provider and authorities
  • keep the logs the system generates for at least six months
  • inform workers' representatives and affected workers before using a high risk system in the workplace
  • tell candidates and employees when a high risk system is used to make or assist decisions about them

Article 86 adds a right for affected people to receive a clear explanation of the role the AI system played in a decision that significantly affects them. An employer that puts its own name on a tool, or substantially modifies it, can become a provider and take on the full set of provider duties.

Who is covered outside the EU

The Act reaches providers that place systems on the EU market wherever they are based, deployers established in the EU, and providers or deployers outside the EU when the system's output is used in the EU. A US company screening applicants for a role in Berlin is in scope for that role. Many global employers will simply apply EU standards to all hiring, which is also how teams have handled the Colorado AI law and New York City's bias audit rule.

Penalties

Using a prohibited practice can cost up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. Breaching most other obligations, including deployer duties for high risk systems, can cost up to EUR 15 million or 3%. Smaller companies face the lower of the two amounts.

A 2026 to 2027 plan for talent teams

  1. Inventory every tool that touches candidates and mark which ones filter, rank, score or target. Include features switched on inside your ATS.
  2. Remove or disable anything that infers emotion from video or voice.
  3. Check each automated step against GDPR Article 22 now: is there meaningful human review before a rejection, and can you answer a candidate's access request?
  4. Ask vendors for their AI Act plan: classification, conformity assessment timing, instructions for use and the logs they will expose to you.
  5. Name the people who will provide human oversight and train them; the softer Article 4 duty still expects documented measures.
  6. Draft candidate notices and a works council briefing so they are ready before December 2027.

Teams that already run AI phone screening or automated ranking should start with step three, because that is where enforcement attention is landing first.

faq.q: Is AI used in recruitment high risk under the EU AI Act?
faq.a: Yes, when it is intended to place targeted job ads, analyse and filter applications or evaluate candidates. Those uses are listed in Annex III, so the high risk obligations apply to them.

faq.q: When do the AI Act's high risk rules apply to hiring tools?
faq.a: From 2 December 2027. The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, moved the date from 2 August 2026.

faq.q: Does anything in the AI Act already apply to recruiting?
faq.a: Yes. The Article 5 bans, including emotion recognition in the workplace, have applied since 2 February 2025, and the AI literacy measures in Article 4 apply as well, in the softer form set by the Omnibus.

faq.q: Does the AI Act apply to US employers?
faq.a: It applies when a US employer deploys AI whose output is used in the EU, for example screening applicants for a job based in the EU.

faq.q: What does GDPR Article 22 mean for AI screening?
faq.a: Candidates have the right not to be rejected by a solely automated decision unless an exception such as explicit consent applies, so meaningful human review before a rejection is the safest default.

faq.q: What are the fines for breaking the AI Act in hiring?
faq.a: Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of global turnover for prohibited practices, and up to EUR 15 million or 3% for most other breaches, including deployer obligations.

title: Will AI replace recruiters? What changes, what stays human, and how to adapt
description: Will AI replace recruiters? A 2026 look at which recruiting tasks AI already handles, which still need people, what Gartner analysts told TA leaders in October, and how recruiters can adapt.
short: No, not as a profession, but AI is replacing large parts of the recruiter's task list. Sourcing, screening for clear criteria, outreach drafting and scheduling are moving to software. Judgment about fit, hiring manager advice, closing offers and fairness oversight remain human work, and they are becoming most of the job.
body:
The honest answer splits in two. AI is not on track to remove the recruiter role, but it is removing chunks of what recruiters spend their days on, and it is doing so faster than most job descriptions are being rewritten. A recruiter whose week is mostly keyword searches, copy and paste messages and calendar juggling is doing work that software now does. A recruiter whose week is mostly advising hiring managers, assessing people and closing candidates is doing work that is getting more valuable, not less.

What AI already does in recruiting

Most of the tasks below were manual a few years ago and are now routine features in recruiting software:

  • Sourcing. AI search reads a role description and returns matching profiles, rather than waiting for a recruiter to build Boolean strings.
  • Screening against clear criteria. Tools rank applications against must have requirements and flag gaps.
  • Outreach drafting and sequencing. Personalized first messages and follow ups are written and sent on a schedule.
  • Scheduling. Interview times are matched across calendars without a coordinator in the loop.
  • Notes and summaries. Interview transcripts become structured scorecards in minutes.

Some products now chain these steps into one agent. Noon, for example, sources candidates against a role brief and runs email and SMS outreach for recruiting teams until a reply turns into a booked call. Tools like this change the unit of work from a single search or message to a whole funnel stage.

What the analysts said in October 2026

At the Gartner HR Symposium/Xpo on 26 October 2026, senior director analyst Jamie Kohn described the pressure clearly, as reported by HR Dive. Application volume has more than doubled in the last two years. The old firewall that kept AI out of candidate screening and assessment is crumbling, and recruiters will use AI whether employers approve it or not. Kohn also said keeping AI permanently out of screening is not sustainable, and that roles that are stable and repeatable, with clear criteria and high scale, are the lower risk place to accelerate it.

Her other point matters more for the replacement question. Recruiters are asked to act strategically, yet the system around them rewards speed and deference to hiring managers on open roles only. Her fix was to measure what employers actually want from recruiters, such as slate quality, time to productivity and candidate confidence. None of those metrics is something a sourcing tool can own on its own.

What stays human

Four parts of recruiting resist automation, and they are the parts hiring managers notice most:

  • Defining the role. Turning a vague request into a brief with real must haves takes a conversation and some pushback.
  • Judging ambiguous fit. When skills are hard to observe or success is hard to define, AI evaluation becomes risky, a point Kohn made directly.
  • Closing. Counteroffers, relocation, family timing and compensation tradeoffs are negotiated person to person.
  • Accountability. Laws such as the Colorado AI Act and the EU AI Act expect humans to oversee automated hiring decisions and answer for them.

Which recruiting jobs are most exposed

Exposure follows the task mix. Sourcer roles built around list building, coordinator roles built around scheduling, and high volume screening desks for repeatable hourly roles will shrink or merge as agents absorb their core tasks. Full cycle recruiters, executive search consultants and agency recruiters who own client relationships are less exposed, because their value sits in judgment and trust. Expect fewer people per requisition rather than no people.

How recruiters can adapt

  • Learn to brief and audit AI tools: write precise criteria, review a sample of rejected candidates and correct the scoring.
  • Move time from searching to advising: bring hiring managers market data, slate comparisons and clear tradeoffs.
  • Own the candidate experience in a world where many applications are AI assisted; verify identity and skills early.
  • Track the metrics Kohn named, such as slate quality and time to productivity, so your impact is visible beyond time to fill.

For a deeper look at how these systems actually make decisions, see our explainers on ATS and AI resume screening and on the AI recruiting assistant.

faq.q: Will AI replace recruiters completely?
faq.a: No. AI is taking over sourcing, screening against clear criteria, outreach drafting and scheduling, but role definition, judging ambiguous fit, closing offers and accountability for hiring decisions remain human work.

faq.q: Which recruiting jobs are most at risk from AI?
faq.a: Roles built mainly around list building, interview scheduling or screening high volumes of applicants for repeatable roles are the most exposed. Full cycle, executive search and client facing agency recruiters are less exposed.

faq.q: How is AI changing recruiting in 2026?
faq.a: Application volume has more than doubled in two years according to a Gartner analyst, and employers are moving AI into screening and assessment, starting with stable, repeatable roles that have clear criteria.

faq.q: What skills do recruiters need to work alongside AI?
faq.a: Writing precise role criteria, auditing AI recommendations, advising hiring managers with market data, verifying candidate identity and skills, and closing offers.

faq.q: Is it still worth becoming a recruiter?
faq.a: Yes, if you build the advisory and judgment side of the job. The task mix is shifting away from manual searching and toward assessment, influence and closing.

title: AI interview scheduling: how it books interviews, where it fails, and what to ask vendors
description: What AI interview scheduling is, how it books, reminds and reschedules over SMS, email and chat, the three ways teams deploy it in 2026, common failure points, and questions to ask vendors.
short: AI interview scheduling lets software book interviews by messaging the candidate directly. It reads interviewer calendars, offers times that fit the team's rules, confirms the booking and handles reminders and reschedules. It saves recruiters hours of back and forth but needs clean calendars, explicit confirmations and a human fallback.
body:
AI interview scheduling is software that books interviews by talking to the candidate directly, in a text thread, email or chat window, instead of making a recruiter trade messages to find a time. It reads the interviewers' calendars, offers slots that fit the rules the team has set, confirms the booking, sends reminders and handles the reschedule when someone cancels. The useful way to think about it: it removes waiting, not judgment. Nobody is being evaluated at this step; what the software decides is only when.

What it replaces

Before automation, booking a single panel interview typically meant a coordinator emailing a candidate for availability, checking four calendars, proposing times, losing a day when one interviewer declined, and starting over. Older self scheduling links fixed part of that by letting the candidate pick from open slots. The AI layer adds conversation on top: the candidate can reply "Thursday after 3 works, but not if it is on site," and the system parses the request, checks constraints and answers in plain language.

How it works, step by step

  1. Trigger. A candidate passes a screen, replies to outreach or is moved to an interview stage in the ATS.
  2. Rules. The system loads the interview plan: who must attend, length, buffers, time zones, working hours and any limits such as no more than two interviews per interviewer per day.
  3. Conversation. It offers times over SMS, email or chat, answers routine questions about location, parking or format, and accepts free text replies.
  4. Booking. It creates the calendar events, video links and confirmations, and writes the result back to the ATS.
  5. Upkeep. It sends reminders, handles reschedules and no shows, and swaps in a backup interviewer from an approved pool when needed.

Where it shows up in 2026

Scheduling is now a standard feature of recruiting suites rather than a separate purchase. Paylocity's Recruiting Optimizer, announced in October 2026, uses conversational AI over web and SMS to book interviews against recruiter defined criteria, and the company claims a 35 percent gain in recruiter productivity in its paid release. In November, HiringDesk.ai launched an assistant for local employers that texts applicants and books interviews without a separate calendar tool. Treat vendor productivity figures as claims to test, not benchmarks. SHRM's guide on using AI to simplify interview scheduling frames the goal as less work for recruiters and less frustration for candidates, which is a fair test for any product.

Three ways teams deploy it

SetupTypical userStrengthWeak spot
Built into the ATS or HCM suiteEnterprise and mid market teamsData stays in one system of recordPanel and multi day loops can be rigid
Standalone scheduling productTeams with complex interview loopsDeep rules for panels, rooms and interviewer loadAnother integration to maintain
Part of an outreach or screening agentHigh volume and outbound sourcing teamsA reply becomes a booked call in the same threadLess control over interviewer pools

The third pattern is growing fastest, because the gap between a candidate saying yes and a time being set is where many are lost. Noon's interview booking assistant is one example: it picks up candidate replies to email and SMS outreach and handles the back and forth. Others pair scheduling with AI phone screening or an AI interviewer that runs the first round itself.

What can go wrong

  • Misread replies. A message like "can't do mornings, sorry" sent to the wrong thread can be booked as a yes. Require explicit confirmation of the final slot.
  • Calendar hygiene. The tool only knows what calendars show. Interviewers who block focus time loosely or forget travel will get double booked.
  • Fairness of access. Candidates without reliable phone or internet access, or who need accommodations, must have a human route. Always include a way to reach a person.
  • Over automation. Senior candidates often expect to hear from a recruiter, not a bot. Many teams automate early stage booking and keep final rounds personal.

Questions to ask a vendor

Ask which calendar systems and ATS it writes back to, how it handles panels and time zones, whether candidates can reply in free text, what happens when it is unsure, and how every message is logged. If the tool also screens or ranks, the scheduling step falls under the same rules as screening; our explainer on the Colorado AI Act and hiring covers what disclosure can involve. For the broader picture of where scheduling sits among recruiting agents, see how recruitment AI works.

faq.q: What is AI interview scheduling?
faq.a: It is software that books interviews by conversing with candidates over text, email or chat, checking interviewer calendars against rules, creating the invite and managing reminders and reschedules.

faq.q: Is AI interview scheduling the same as a self scheduling link?
faq.a: No. A link lets candidates pick from open slots. AI scheduling also understands free text replies, answers routine questions and rebooks automatically when plans change.

faq.q: Does AI interview scheduling make hiring decisions?
faq.a: Not on its own. Scheduling decides when an interview happens, not who advances. If the same product screens or ranks candidates, that part may be covered by AI hiring laws.

faq.q: What should I check before buying an AI scheduler?
faq.a: Check ATS and calendar write back, panel and time zone handling, how it treats uncertain replies, message logging, accessibility and an easy route to a human.

title: AI for staffing agencies: where it saves recruiter hours, where it adds risk, and how desks roll it out
description: A plain English explainer of AI for staffing agencies in 2026: the five jobs it does on a staffing desk, how it differs from corporate recruiting AI, the risks for candidates and clients, and a rollout plan.
short: AI for staffing agencies means software that sources, matches, contacts and screens candidates for client orders, and keeps a large database of past candidates working. It matters more for agencies than for corporate teams because agency revenue depends on speed to submit. The main risks are biased matching, poor candidate communication and data use the client never agreed to.
body:
Why would a staffing firm care about AI more than a corporate recruiting team does? Because an agency only gets paid when its candidate is the one hired, and on most contract orders the first strong submittal wins. AI for staffing agencies is software that shortens the time between a client order and a qualified candidate in front of the client: it finds people, matches them to the order, contacts them, asks the first screening questions and updates the record. The American Staffing Association's staffing index showed staffing jobs in October 2026 running 2.4 percent above the same period of 2025, so desks are being asked to fill more orders without hiring more recruiters.

How agency AI differs from corporate recruiting AI

A corporate team hires for one employer and one brand. An agency recruiter may work twenty open orders for eight clients at once, and the same candidate can fit three of them. That changes what the software has to do. Matching has to run across every open order, not just one requisition. The database is the main asset, since agencies keep years of candidates who have already worked an assignment. And communication has to keep candidates warm between assignments, because a good contractor who finishes a job on Friday should hear about the next one before Monday.

The five jobs AI does on a staffing desk

Database matching. When an order arrives, the system scores existing candidates against it and surfaces people who are available and nearby. This is usually the fastest return, because the candidates are already known to the firm.

Sourcing new candidates. For orders the database cannot fill, AI search tools look across public profiles and job boards and build a list ranked by fit.

Outreach. Messages go out by email and text, personalized to the order, with follow ups if there is no reply. Some agencies use the outreach built into their ATS; others use dedicated email and SMS outreach software for staffing desks such as Noon.

Screening. A chat or phone assistant asks the knockout questions: availability, pay rate, certifications, commute. Our explainer on AI phone screening covers how those calls work.

Redeployment and admin. AI drafts submittal summaries, updates statuses and flags contractors whose assignment ends soon so the desk can line up the next one.

What the big platforms now include

Staffing ATS vendors have built much of this in. Bullhorn's site describes Amplify digital workers that handle sourcing, screening and outreach, an Amplify Chat assistant inside the ATS, and Search and Match with AI relevancy scoring, and claims 80 percent faster time to hire for firms using them. Treat vendor figures like that as a starting hypothesis to test on your own orders, not a forecast.

Where it adds risk

Three risks are specific to agencies. First, bias: a matching model trained on who clients accepted in the past can repeat the client's past preferences. The ASA's Workforce Monitor found that 49 percent of employed US job seekers believe AI tools used in recruiting are more biased than humans, so candidates are watching. Second, consent and data use: candidates gave their details to the agency, and clients may restrict how their order data is processed. Third, over messaging: an automated sequence that texts a contractor about every loosely matched order will get the number blocked. Our guide chapter on bias, regulation and candidate rights covers the laws that apply, including the Colorado AI Act.

A rollout plan that works

Start with database matching on one desk for 30 days and measure submittals per order and time to first submittal against the previous month. Add automated outreach next, with caps on messages per candidate per week and an easy opt out. Add AI screening last, once recruiters trust the matching, and always route edge cases to a person. Write down which decisions the software may make and which only a recruiter makes, then share that with clients who ask. For a wider checklist, see how to evaluate recruitment AI.

Will it replace agency recruiters?

Not the parts clients pay for. Clients pay for judgment about who will show up, fit the team and stay the assignment, and for the relationship when something goes wrong. AI takes the searching, first messages and data entry. The argument is laid out in more detail in will AI replace recruiters.

faq.q: What is AI for staffing agencies?
faq.a: Software that matches, sources, contacts and screens candidates for client orders and keeps the agency's candidate database active, so recruiters submit qualified people faster.

faq.q: Which part of AI should a staffing agency adopt first?
faq.a: Database matching, because it works on candidates the agency already knows and shows results within weeks. Outreach automation and AI screening usually follow.

faq.q: Is AI matching biased?
faq.a: It can be. Models that learn from past client decisions can repeat past preferences, so agencies should test outcomes by group and keep a human in final decisions.

faq.q: How do candidates feel about AI in recruiting?
faq.a: The ASA Workforce Monitor found 49 percent of employed US job seekers think AI recruiting tools are more biased than human recruiters, so clear disclosure and a human contact matter.

faq.q: Do staffing ATS platforms include AI?
faq.a: Many now do. Bullhorn, for example, describes AI digital workers for sourcing, screening and outreach, plus AI search and match inside its ATS.

title: Deepfake job candidates: how AI faked interviews work and how hiring teams catch them
seoTitle: Deepfake Job Candidates and Deepfake Interviews Explained
description: A plain English explainer of deepfake job candidates in 2026: what they are, why remote hiring made them common, real cases from KnowBe4 and Microsoft, interview warning signs and verification steps that do not punish real applicants.
short: A deepfake job candidate is an applicant whose face, voice, identity documents or credentials have been faked or altered with AI so someone else can be hired. Cases range from AI polished photos to live face swaps and stand in interviewers. The best defenses are identity verification tied to payroll, consistent records across rounds and careful onboarding, with a person making every rejection decision.
body:
Picture a hiring manager on a video call with a strong software engineering candidate. The answers are fluent, the camera is on and the face matches the photo on the application. The day the company laptop arrives, it starts loading malware. That is not a thought experiment. It is roughly what the security training company KnowBe4 described publicly in 2024: it hired a remote engineer after four video interviews, background checks and reference calls, and the profile photo turned out to be an AI altered stock image. The Mac it shipped to the new hire started loading malware as soon as it arrived, and its security team caught the activity on July 15, 2024.

What a deepfake candidate is

A deepfake job candidate is an applicant whose identity, face, voice or credentials have been fabricated or altered with AI so that someone else can get hired. The term covers a spectrum. At the light end is a real person using an AI enhanced headshot and an AI written resume. In the middle is a proxy: one person interviews and a different person does the job. At the far end is live face swapping or voice changing during the interview itself, so the hiring team never sees or hears the real applicant.

Why it is happening now

Three things lined up. Remote hiring means many employers never meet a new hire in person. Generative AI made convincing photos, documents and scripts cheap. And for some groups the payoff is large. Microsoft's threat intelligence team reported in June 2025 that North Korea has placed thousands of remote IT workers in software and web development jobs as a revenue scheme, that these workers use AI to swap images in stolen identity documents and polish their photos, and that they have used voice changing software. Microsoft said it suspended 3,000 Outlook and Hotmail accounts created by those workers.

Deepfake voice is not limited to hiring. Pindrop, which sells voice and meeting deepfake detection, says in its 2025 Voice Intelligence and Security Report that 2.6 million fraud events were reported, and it now markets a product for catching fake job candidates in video meetings.

How the fraud usually works

Stage one: the application. A real or stolen identity, a resume tuned to the job description with AI, and a profile photo that may be generated. References are often friends or accomplices with matching stories.

Stage two: the interview. The candidate may keep video off, blame a poor connection, or use a face swap filter. Some interviews are taken by a skilled stand in while a different person later does the work. Real time AI assistants can also feed answers to technical questions.

Stage three: onboarding. Equipment is shipped to an address that does not match the identity, sometimes a so called laptop farm where hardware is kept online for remote access from abroad. Payroll goes to accounts set up for the scheme.

Warning signs during interviews

No single signal proves fraud, and many have innocent explanations, so look for patterns. Lip movement that drifts out of sync with audio, or a face that blurs when the candidate turns or raises a hand, can point to a live filter. Long pauses before every answer, especially on follow ups, can mean someone is reading AI output. A candidate who resists turning on the camera across every round, or whose voice changes between calls, deserves a closer look. Mismatches between the stated location, time zone, phone number and shipping address are among the most useful signals because they are hard to fake together.

What employers can do

Microsoft's guidance is practical: be especially careful with workers supplied through staffing companies, check resumes for internal consistency, and use video calls to confirm identity. Building on that, many teams now add a few low cost steps. Verify government ID against a live selfie at the offer stage rather than at the end of onboarding. Ask one interviewer to request a simple unscripted action on camera, such as standing up or showing the room. Call references on numbers you find independently. Ship equipment only to an address that matches verified identity documents, and watch for remote access tools in the first weeks.

Detection software is a second layer, not a substitute. Vendors now score video and voice for signs of synthesis, and some AI interviewer platforms flag identity mismatches between rounds. Treat their output as a reason to verify, never as an automatic rejection.

Do not punish real candidates

Over correction has a cost. Candidates with poor connections, disabilities that affect speech or appearance, or accents that confuse transcription can trip naive checks. Tell candidates in advance what identity checks you run and why, give them a way to verify without a live camera if they need an accommodation, and keep a person in every rejection decision. Our guide chapter on bias, regulation and candidate rights covers the disclosure rules that apply to automated screening, and our explainer on ATS and AI resume screening explains where automated filters already sit in the process.

Where this is heading

Face and voice synthesis will keep improving, so checks that rely on spotting visual glitches will age quickly. The durable defenses are the boring ones: verified identity tied to payroll, consistent records across the hiring process, and onboarding controls that limit what a new account can reach in its first month. Recruiters who already run AI phone screening or structured interviews have an advantage, because consistent questions make inconsistent answers easier to see.

faq.q: What is a deepfake job interview?
faq.a: An interview in which the candidate uses AI to alter their face or voice in real time, or has someone else appear in their place, so the employer hires a person other than the one it thinks it interviewed.

faq.q: How common are deepfake candidates?
faq.a: There is no reliable industry wide count. Microsoft reported in 2025 that North Korea alone has placed thousands of remote IT workers using AI altered identities, and security vendors now sell products aimed specifically at fake candidates.

faq.q: How can I tell if a candidate is using a deepfake?
faq.a: Look for audio and lip sync drift, blurring when the face moves, repeated refusal to use video, voices that change between calls and mismatches between location, phone number and shipping address. Confirm suspicions with identity verification rather than rejecting on one signal.

faq.q: Can AI detect deepfake candidates?
faq.a: Detection tools can score video and voice for signs of synthesis and flag mismatches between interview rounds. They work best as a prompt for human verification, not as the final decision.

faq.q: Is it legal to verify a candidate's identity on video?
faq.a: Generally yes, when applied consistently and disclosed in advance, but rules on biometric data and automated decisions vary by state and country. Check local requirements and offer an accommodation route.

title: Skills based hiring and AI: how the two fit together, and where they clash
seoTitle: Skills Based Hiring and AI Explained
description: A plain English explainer of skills based hiring and AI in 2026: what skills inference, AI written job descriptions and automated assessments do, what survey data says about dropped degree requirements, the risks of proxy creep and the rules that apply.
short: Skills based hiring evaluates candidates on demonstrated abilities instead of degrees or titles. AI supports it by inferring skills from work histories, rewriting job descriptions as skills and running assessments and structured interviews at scale. It only works when the AI widens the pool and decisions rest on tested skills that are checked against job performance.
body:
Skills based hiring means judging candidates on what they can do rather than on proxies such as degrees, job titles or years of experience. AI helps with that in two ways: it can read a résumé or profile and infer skills that are not spelled out, and it can run assessments and structured interviews at a scale no recruiting team could manage by hand. Used carefully, the combination widens the pool. Used carelessly, it rebuilds the old filters with new labels.

What changed in the last few years

The shift away from degree requirements is real but uneven. TestGorilla's State of Skills-Based Hiring 2025 survey found that 53% of employers had dropped degree requirements, up from 30% a year earlier, and that 65% were using AI somewhere in their hiring process. The same report found 63% of employers saying great talent was harder to find than the year before, which is part of why the pool is being widened.

Announcements and practice are not the same thing. A February 2024 study from the Burning Glass Institute and Harvard Business School, Skills-Based Hiring: The Long Road from Pronouncements to Practice, found that many companies had announced they were dropping degree requirements, but sustained changes in who they actually hired remained elusive for most. Removing a line from a job ad does little if the screening step that follows still rewards the same backgrounds.

Where AI fits in a skills based process

Skills inference

Modern screening models map a work history to a skills taxonomy. A warehouse lead who scheduled shifts and trained new hires can be tagged with workforce planning and coaching even if those words never appear. This is the part that can help candidates without degrees, because it credits experience that a keyword filter would miss. Our explainer on ATS résumé parsing and AI screening covers how those models read documents.

Job descriptions written as skills

Generative AI can rewrite a requirement list into the tasks and skills the job actually needs. That makes the posting easier to match against inferred skills, and it forces the hiring manager to say what matters. The weak point is that models reproduce the patterns in whatever text they learned from, so a human still needs to cut inflated requirements.

Assessments and structured interviews

Work samples, short skills tests and structured interviews with fixed rubrics are the strongest evidence in a skills based process. AI makes them cheaper to run: an AI interviewer can ask every candidate the same questions, and scoring tools can grade answers against a rubric. Consistency is the benefit. The risk is a score that looks precise but has never been checked against job performance.

Ways it goes wrong

  • Proxy creep. A model trained on past hires may learn that certain schools or employers predict success and quietly weight them, undoing the point of dropping degrees.
  • Taxonomy gaps. Skills common in trades, care work or military roles are often thin in commercial taxonomies, so the model misses them.
  • Over automated rejection. If the AI score becomes a hard cutoff, people with unusual paths are filtered out before anyone looks.
  • Candidate polish. Applicants increasingly use AI to rewrite résumés, so self reported skills need a test or interview behind them.

Rules that apply

Automated tools that score or rank candidates are regulated in a growing number of places. New York City requires bias audits for automated employment decision tools, the EU AI Act classes most recruitment AI as high risk, and Colorado has passed its own law on high risk AI systems. Skills based tools are not exempt because their intent is fairer. Our guides to the EU AI Act and the Colorado AI Act explain the obligations, and the chapter on bias, regulation and candidate rights covers notice and appeal.

A practical starting point

  1. Pick one high volume role and list the five skills that separate strong performers, with the hiring manager.
  2. Remove degree and years of experience requirements that do not map to those skills.
  3. Use AI skills inference to widen the first pass, not to reject.
  4. Add a short work sample or structured interview scored on a written rubric.
  5. After six months, compare performance and retention of hires with and without the old credentials, and check pass rates across groups.

That loop is what turns a policy statement into a process. Without the measurement step, neither the skills label nor the AI layer proves anything.

faq.q: What is skills based hiring?
faq.a: It is an approach that evaluates candidates on demonstrated abilities, through work samples, tests and structured interviews, instead of using degrees, titles or years of experience as the main filter.

faq.q: How does AI support skills based hiring?
faq.a: AI can infer skills from work histories, rewrite job descriptions around tasks and skills, and run assessments or structured interviews consistently for every applicant.

faq.q: Can AI make skills based hiring less fair?
faq.a: Yes. Models trained on past hires can learn proxies such as school or former employer. Audit pass rates across groups and keep a human review before rejection.

faq.q: Do employers still drop degree requirements in 2026?
faq.a: Many do. TestGorilla's 2025 survey found 53% of employers had removed degree requirements, but research from the Burning Glass Institute and Harvard Business School shows actual hiring patterns change more slowly than postings.

faq.q: Is skills based hiring regulated?
faq.a: The approach itself is not, but AI tools that score or rank candidates fall under rules such as New York City's bias audit law, the EU AI Act and Colorado's AI Act.

title: AI and candidate experience: where automation helps applicants, and where it drives them away
description: A plain English explainer on AI and candidate experience in 2026: what the Greenhouse candidate survey found about silent rejections and AI interviews, where chatbots, schedulers and screeners help or hurt, and practical rules for keeping applicants' trust.
short: AI affects candidate experience at every step, from careers page chatbots to screening models and AI interviews. It helps when it speeds up scheduling, answers questions and gives every applicant a structured first conversation. It hurts when it rejects people silently or decides without human review. Transparency, status updates and a human owner for each decision keep candidates' trust.
body:
Does AI make applying for a job better or worse for the person on the other side? The honest answer in 2026 is both, depending on where in the process it sits. Candidate experience is the sum of everything an applicant sees, hears and waits for between finding a job ad and getting an answer. AI now touches almost every one of those moments, from the chatbot on the careers page to the screening model that ranks the application and the voice interviewer that asks the first questions.

What candidates say right now

The clearest recent data comes from the 2026 Greenhouse Future of Hiring Candidate Report, which surveyed more than 2,800 job seekers in five countries, including 1,200 in the United States. Among the U.S. respondents, 81% had been rejected from a job in the past year without speaking to anyone at the company, human or AI, and 31% said it happens often or almost always. That silence is the biggest candidate experience problem, and it predates AI.

Candidates are using AI too. The same survey found 77% of U.S. job seekers used AI in their search, while 60% had changed or considered changing how they write so their applications would not be mistaken for AI generated text. And 62% had tried tactics to get past automated screening, including 40% who added skills or keywords they do not have. Both sides are now optimizing for machines, which makes the application itself less useful as a signal.

Where AI improves the experience

The strongest case for AI is speed and response. A scheduling assistant that offers interview slots within minutes removes days of email back and forth. A chatbot that answers questions about pay, location or visa sponsorship at midnight saves the candidate a guess. And automated status updates can end the black hole problem, if a team chooses to send them.

AI interviews are a more surprising bright spot. Greenhouse found that 48% of U.S. candidates had taken an AI interview in the past year and 70% of them said it let them show their skills well. Only 7% said they would refuse an AI led interview outright. A structured first conversation available at any hour gives every applicant a chance to be heard, which is more than a résumé filter offers. Our AI interviewer explainer covers how these tools score answers.

Where it makes things worse

The damage shows up when AI is used to reject quickly without explanation. Automated screens that drop applicants on keywords encourage keyword stuffing, punish career changers whose experience is described differently and leave people with no idea why they lost. Our explainer on résumé parsing and AI screening walks through how those filters read an application.

Trust is the other weak point. In Pew Research Center's 2023 survey, Americans opposed AI making final hiring decisions by 71% to 7%, even though 47% thought AI would do better than people at evaluating every applicant the same way. Candidates accept AI as a helper. They do not accept it as the judge.

Practices that keep candidates on side

  • Tell people when AI is involved. Say in the posting and the invitation which steps use AI and what it evaluates.
  • Keep a person on every rejection after an interview. AI can draft the message; a recruiter should own the decision.
  • Send a status update at every stage. Automation makes this nearly free, so silence is a choice.
  • Offer an alternative. Give candidates who need an accommodation a route to a human interviewer.
  • Audit outcomes. Compare pass rates across groups at each AI step, as the rules in our candidate rights chapter increasingly require.

The bottom line

AI improves candidate experience when it adds speed, answers and a fair first conversation, and it harms it when it becomes a silent filter. The teams that come out ahead use automation to respond to every applicant and keep people accountable for the decisions that matter.

faq.q: How does AI affect candidate experience?
faq.a: It can shorten waits, answer questions instantly and give every applicant a structured interview, but it can also reject people without explanation. The effect depends on whether teams use it to respond to candidates or only to filter them.

faq.q: Do candidates like AI interviews?
faq.a: Many accept them. In Greenhouse's 2026 survey, 70% of U.S. candidates who took an AI interview said it let them demonstrate their skills well, and only 7% said they would refuse one outright.

faq.q: Should employers tell candidates they use AI?
faq.a: Yes. Disclosure builds trust, and a growing number of laws require notice when automated tools are used to evaluate applicants.

faq.q: What is the biggest candidate experience problem in 2026?
faq.a: Silence. Greenhouse found 81% of U.S. job seekers had been rejected in the past year without speaking to anyone at the company.

faq.q: Can AI make final hiring decisions?
faq.a: It can be configured to, but most candidates oppose it and regulators increasingly expect human review. Use AI to inform decisions, not to make them.

faq.q: Which AI tools improve candidate experience fastest?
faq.a: Interview scheduling assistants and careers page chatbots usually show results first, because they cut waiting time without changing who gets hired.

title: AI bias in hiring: where it comes from, what the research shows and how employers measure it
description: A plain English explainer on AI bias in hiring: how training data, proxies and language models create unequal outcomes, what 2024 audits of résumé screening models found, how the four fifths rule works and practical steps to reduce bias.
short: AI bias in hiring is unequal treatment of candidates by screening, ranking or interview software because of a protected trait or a proxy for one. It usually comes from historical hiring data, proxy variables and associations inside language models. Employers detect it by comparing selection rates between groups, commonly with the four fifths rule, and reduce it with regular audits, job based rubrics and human review of rejections.
body:
AI bias in hiring is what happens when a screening, ranking or interview tool treats candidates differently because of a protected trait such as race, sex, age or disability, or because of something that stands in for one. The software does not need to see a candidate's race to produce a racial gap. It only needs to learn from data where that gap already exists.

Where the bias comes from

Historical training data. A model trained on past hiring decisions learns the preferences of past hiring managers, good and bad. The best known example is the experimental résumé tool Amazon abandoned after it learned to downgrade applications that mentioned women's organizations, as Reuters reported in 2018.

Proxies. Postcodes, college names, gaps in employment, club memberships and even word choice can correlate with protected traits. Removing the name field rarely removes the signal.

Language models themselves. General purpose models absorb associations from the text they are trained on, and those associations show up when the model is asked to compare candidates.

How the tool is used. A cut off set too high, a knockout question that screens out people with caregiving gaps, or a video tool that struggles with some accents can all create unequal outcomes even when the underlying model is reasonable.

What the research found

Two peer reviewed studies from 2024 tested this directly. In an audit by Kyra Wilson and Aylin Caliskan, presented at the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society, researchers ran more than 500 public résumés against 500 job descriptions across nine occupations using text embedding models of the kind used for retrieval. The models favored résumés with White associated names in 85.1% of tests and résumés with female associated names in only 11.1%, and Black male names were disadvantaged in up to 100% of comparisons.

A separate ACL 2024 study by Haozhe An and colleagues asked language models to write acceptance or rejection emails to applicants whose only difference was their first name. The models were more likely to accept White applicants than Hispanic applicants in many settings, but the pattern shifted from one prompt template to the next. That instability is the practical lesson: you cannot assume a model is fair because it was fair on one test.

How employers measure it

The standard first check in the United States is the four fifths rule from the federal Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures. Divide each group's selection rate at a step by the rate of the group selected most often. A ratio below 0.8 is generally treated as evidence of adverse impact and a reason to look harder. If 50% of men pass an AI screen but only 35% of women do, the impact ratio is 0.70, which fails.

Impact ratios are a smoke alarm, not a verdict. Small samples make them noisy, and a passing ratio overall can hide a failing one for a subgroup, such as older women. Good audits look at each step separately, test intersectional groups, and repeat after every model or configuration change.

The rules employers now face

Existing anti discrimination law already applies to AI decisions: an employer is responsible for the outcome whether a person or a vendor's model made the call. On top of that, newer rules add specific duties, from New York City's annual bias audits for automated employment decision tools to Colorado's state law and the EU's treatment of recruitment AI as high risk. Our chapter on bias, regulation and candidate rights summarizes them, and we cover the Colorado AI Act and the EU AI Act in their own explainers.

Reducing bias in practice

  • Ask vendors for their audit. Request the impact ratios by group, the date of the analysis, who ran it and what data it used.
  • Run your own numbers. Your applicant pool differs from the vendor's test set, so compute selection rates on your own data at least once a quarter.
  • Score against the job, not the past. Rubrics built from the skills a role needs are less prone to copying old patterns than models trained on who was hired before.
  • Keep humans on adverse decisions. Let AI sort and summarize, and require a person to confirm every rejection after the first screen.
  • Give candidates a route out. Offer an alternative process for anyone who needs an accommodation, and tell applicants when AI is used.

The bottom line

AI can make hiring more consistent than tired humans reading the hundredth application, but consistency is not the same as fairness. Bias enters through data, proxies and configuration, and it changes when the model changes. Treat measurement as an ongoing job and keep a person accountable for the outcome.

faq.q: What is AI bias in hiring?
faq.a: It is when AI recruiting software produces different outcomes for candidates based on race, sex, age, disability or another protected trait, directly or through proxies such as postcode or college.

faq.q: Can removing names and photos stop AI hiring bias?
faq.a: It helps but rarely solves it, because other fields such as schools, addresses, employment gaps and phrasing can still correlate with protected traits.

faq.q: What is the four fifths rule?
faq.a: A screening test from the US Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures. If a group's selection rate is less than 80% of the rate for the most selected group, that is generally treated as evidence of adverse impact.

faq.q: Is the employer or the vendor responsible for biased AI decisions?
faq.a: Under US anti discrimination law the employer remains responsible for its hiring outcomes, even when a vendor's tool made the recommendation. Contracts can share costs, but not the legal duty.

faq.q: How often should AI hiring tools be audited?
faq.a: At least annually where the law requires it, and in practice after every model update or configuration change and on a regular schedule, such as quarterly, using your own applicant data.
